  "core_problem": "LLMs generate long-form outputs where hallucinated claims are expressed with the same high confidence as factual ones. Existing approaches either detect hallucinations at claim level without calibrating expressed confidence (Han et al., EMNLP 2025 — binary probes + neuron clamping), calibrate confidence only at response level for short-form QA (Ji et al., EMNLP 2025; Miao & Ungar, 2026), or require multi-stage training of the base model (CURE, April 2026; CAG, May 2026). No existing method performs claim-level calibrated uncertainty expression in long-form generation without base model training.",
  "opportunity": "Three recent results create a convergent opportunity: (1) Han et al. (EMNLP Findings 2025) showed lightweight linear probes on hidden states detect claim-level factuality in long-form generation, matching expensive multi-sample methods at up to 100× fewer FLOPs — but their neuron clamping intervention is binary (suppress/allow), not calibrated; (2) Miao & Ungar (March 2026) discovered that internal accuracy and verbalized confidence are nearly orthogonal linear features (cosine similarity < 0.04), meaning models internally know when they're wrong but fail to express this — and that adaptive CAA steering along these directions achieves 44–7× calibration improvement, but only for response-level QA; (3) Kumaran et al. (March 2026) demonstrated that confidence representations are cached at answer-adjacent positions before verbalization, enabling real-time detection during generation. Combining these — reading claim-level accuracy signals via probes during generation, then steering verbalized confidence to match — is unexplored and fills the specific gap between binary hallucination detection and calibrated confidence expression at claim granularity in long-form outputs. The required components (FActScore decomposition, linear probe training, contrastive direction extraction) are well-documented with available implementations, making this feasible within a focused experimental budget.",

Their neuron clamping causally reduces hallucinations by fixing activations of factuality-correlated neurons — but this is a binary intervention (suppress or allow) that does not produce calibrated verbal uncertainty expression. Obeso et al. (arXiv 2509.03531, 2025) trains entity-level probes for real-time streaming hallucination detection in long-form generation (AUC 0.90 on Llama-3.3-70B) — detection only, no calibrated steering.\n\n**Closest prior work — calibrated confidence steering:** Miao & Ungar (arXiv 2603.25052, March 2026) discovered that calibration accuracy and verbalized confidence are orthogonal linear features, and proposed two-stage adaptive CAA steering that reads internal accuracy and steers verbalized output to match, achieving ECE improvements from 14.9→3.7 (Llama-3.1-8B) and 35.1→3.3 (Mistral-7B) — but only for response-level short-form QA on 7–8B models. Ji et al. (EMNLP 2025) discovered the Verbal Uncertainty Feature (VUF) and proposed MUC with ~30% reduction in confident hallucinations — also response-level, short-form, on ≤8B models, with Qwen2.5 showing 'significantly less sensitivity' to steering.\n\n**Mechanistic understanding:** 'How do LLMs Compute Verbal Confidence?' (arXiv 2603.17839, March 2026) provides convergent evidence that confidence representations emerge at answer-adjacent positions via cached retrieval, supporting the feasibility of online detection during generation.\n\n**Training-free steering baselines:** SteerConf (NeurIPS 2025) does prompt-based training-free confidence steering via multi-prompt aggregation. ACT (WWW 2025) applies tuning-free diverse steering vectors with adaptive intensity for truthfulness, scaling to 65B. SteerMoE (arXiv 2509.09660, 2025) steers MoE models via expert (de)activation.\n\n**Claim-level long-form calibration (training-based):** CURE (arXiv 2604.12046, April 2026) uses multi-stage training to teach claim-level confidence reasoning, improving accuracy by up to 39.9%. CAG (arXiv 2605.01749, May 2026) achieves up to 13% factuality gain via training-based calibration-aware generation. Both require base model fine-tuning or RL.\n\n**Post-generation claim-level approaches:** CSS (arXiv 2604.17487, April 2026) decomposes answers into claims and backs off uncertain ones using external verifiers. Selective Abstraction (arXiv 2602.11908, February 2026) replaces low-confidence atoms with confident abstractions.\n\n**Residual-stream anomaly detection:** PCNET (arXiv 2605.05953, May 2026) uses probabilistic circuits on residual streams for hallucination detection + contrastive decoding, reaching up to 99% AUROC — but targets short-form QA and changes content (different token selection) rather than expressing calibrated uncertainty.\n\n**Gap:** No existing work combines claim-level factuality probing (à la Han et al.) with calibrated activation steering along the verbalized-confidence direction (à la Miao & Ungar) in a single-pass, online framework for long-form generation. This intersection — reading internal accuracy per-claim and steering verbalized confidence to match during generation — is the contribution space.",
  "approach": "We propose Read-and-Steer (RaS), a single-pass framework for claim-level calibrated uncertainty expression in long-form generation. The system reads internal accuracy signals per-claim via lightweight probes and steers verbalized confidence to match via targeted activation intervention, producing naturally hedged language for uncertain claims while leaving confident-and-correct claims untouched.\n\n**Offline Stage 1 — Factuality Probe Training (~5h H100, one-time per model):** Generate long-form outputs (biographies, factual descriptions) from the target model, decompose into atomic claims using FActScore/OpenFActScore decomposition, verify claim factuality against knowledge sources. Extract hidden states at each claim's token span across multiple layers (following Han et al.'s layer-group methodology). Train lightweight linear probes (logistic regression on span-aggregated hidden states) to predict continuous factuality confidence scores. Unlike Han et al.'s binary factuality labels, we train on soft labels derived from verification confidence, enabling graded uncertainty estimation.\n\n**Offline Stage 2 — Verbalized-Confidence Direction Extraction (~2h H100, one-time per model):** Extract a verbalized-confidence steering direction via contrastive activation pairs: generate matched claim pairs where the same factual content is expressed with high confidence ('X was born in Y') vs. hedged uncertainty ('X was reportedly born in Y, though I am not certain'). The mean activation difference yields the steering direction, following the contrastive methodology from Ji et al. (VUF) and Miao & Ungar (CAA). Critically, this direction is orthogonal to the accuracy direction read by probes (per Miao & Ungar's finding), meaning steering verbalized confidence does not corrupt the accuracy signal.\n\n**Online Stage — Probe-Guided Steering During Generation:** During autoregressive generation: (1) At each generated token, run the factuality probe on its hidden states — this is a single matrix-vector multiplication with negligible overhead. (2) Maintain a running mean probe score over the current sentence span using a sliding window. (3) At sentence boundaries (detected from generated punctuation — periods, newlines — which are trivially available during generation), evaluate the accumulated probe score against a calibrated threshold. (4) If the probe indicates internal uncertainty (score below threshold) while the generation shows no hedging markers, apply a steering offset along the extracted verbalized-confidence direction on subsequent tokens, with steering magnitude α proportional to the miscalibration gap: α = β × max(0, threshold − probe_score), where β is calibrated on a held-out validation set. (b) Single-pass online monitoring eliminates the two-pass chicken-and-egg problem identified for the original CL-MUC approach — no position-aligned regeneration needed. (c) Continuous calibrated steering (not binary neuron clamping) produces graded hedging proportional to internal uncertainty, distinguishing this from Han et al.'s binary intervention. Llama 3.1-8B as secondary validation (well-studied for VUF/steering, enables direct comparison with Ji et al. and Miao & Ungar baselines). Llama 4 Scout is excluded — its MoE architecture (109B total, 17B active, 16 experts) makes linear feature identification fundamentally harder due to per-token expert routing.\n\n**Benchmarks:** FActScore (biography generation, primary) and LongFact (diverse long-form factuality). Metrics: claim-level ECE, Brier score (calibration quality), AUROC (uncertainty detection), FActScore/factual precision (to verify steering does not degrade content quality), and MT-Bench fluency subset (to verify generation quality preservation).\n\n**Comparisons:** (1) Unsteered baseline, (2) Han et al.'s probes + neuron clamping (closest representation-based method), (3) CURE (closest training-based method, if reproducible), (4) Ablations: probe-only detection without steering, uniform steering without probe guidance, VUF-only steering (Ji et al.'s original method applied per-claim), varying layers for probe extraction, steering strength sensitivity.",

## Reviewer feedback (round 2)
Issues: ["CRITICAL — Qwen3.5-27B architecture mismatch: Qwen3.5-27B uses a hybrid Gated DeltaNet + attention architecture (3:1 ratio). 75% of layers are DeltaNet (linear attention), fundamentally different from standard transformer attention. Linear probes, contrastive activation directions, and steering techniques were developed and validated ONLY on standard transformer architectures. TransformerLens does not support DeltaNet layers. The proposal claims Qwen3.5-27B is 'confirmed viable for activation steering' — this is false and unverified. The entire primary experimental setup may fail on day 1.", "CRITICAL — Unverified scaling assumption: Miao & Ungar's accuracy-confidence orthogonality (cosine similarity < 0.04) was demonstrated ONLY on 7-8B standard transformers (Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B, Qwen2.5-7B) on short-form QA. They explicitly state: 'Whether the linear encoding findings hold at larger scales remains open. Evaluation is restricted to question-answering tasks; extending to open-ended generation would require rethinking how the probe target is constructed.' RaS critically depends on this orthogonality holding at 27B scale in long-form generation — this is an assumption, not a validated property.", "MISSING COMPETITOR — CORAL (arXiv 2602.06022, Feb 2026): From the SAME Miao & Ungar group. Trains MLP probes on residual stream activations to predict correctness, then steers model behavior at inference time — essentially the same probe→steer pipeline concept. Evaluates on MCQA with 7B models. Must be cited and differentiated as same-group prior work.", "MISSING COMPETITOR — CLAS (arXiv 2604.24693, April 2026): Contextual Linear Activation Steering uses probe-derived steering vectors with dynamic, context-dependent strength. RaS's α = β × max(0, threshold − probe_score) is conceptually similar to CLAS's adaptive steering strength. Must be cited.", "MISSING COMPETITOR — ITI (NeurIPS 2023, Li et al.): Inference-Time Intervention — the foundational work that uses linear probes to identify truthful directions in attention heads and steers during generation. The probe→steer-during-generation paradigm originates here. Not cited.", "MISSING COMPETITOR — ActCab/CoDec (EMNLP 2024): Trains a linear layer on LM last-layer activations for confidence calibration, then uses confidence-guided decoding to elicit truthful answers. Same conceptual pipeline (activation-based calibration → guided generation). Not cited.", "Timeline risk: EMNLP 2026 ARR deadline is May 25, 2026 — 10 days away. With the DeltaNet architecture risk likely requiring a pivot to Llama 3.1-8B only (reducing the paper to a direct comparison with Miao & Ungar on the same 8B model), this is not enough time to produce competitive results. AAAI 2027 (July 28) is more realistic.", "Qwen2.5 sensitivity acknowledged but not addressed: Miao & Ungar note that Qwen2.5-7B shows 'significantly less sensitivity' to VUF steering compared to Llama and Mistral. If Qwen models are inherently less responsive to this type of steering, the Qwen3.5-27B results may be disappointing even if the architecture challenge is resolved."]
Feedback: The core idea — combining Han et al.'s claim-level probes with Miao & Ungar's calibrated confidence steering in single-pass long-form generation — addresses a genuine gap. But there are critical issues that must be resolved:

**1. Replace Qwen3.5-27B as primary model (HIGHEST PRIORITY):**
Qwen3.5-27B's hybrid DeltaNet architecture (75% linear attention layers) is untested territory for linear probes and activation steering. All prior work validated these techniques on standard transformer architectures. Options:
- **Best option**: Use Llama 3.1-70B (standard transformer, well-studied, large enough to be compelling) as primary, with Llama 3.1-8B as validation for direct comparison to Miao & Ungar. This requires ~2× the compute of 8B but fits within 200 H100-hours if you drop Qwen entirely.
- **Alternative**: Use Qwen2.5-32B (standard transformer architecture, unlike Qwen3.5). But note Qwen2.5 shows reduced sensitivity to confidence steering per Miao & Ungar.
- **Risky fallback**: Keep Qwen3.5-27B but acknowledge it as an architectural exploration, not 'confirmed viable.' Run a 5h pilot on DeltaNet-layer probing before committing.

**2. Cite all missing competitors and sharpen differentiation:**
Add CORAL (same group as Miao & Ungar — probe→steer on MCQA), CLAS (dynamic steering strength from probes), ITI (foundational probe→steer work, NeurIPS 2023), and ActCab/CoDec (activation calibration + guided decoding, EMNLP 2024). Your differentiation should be: all prior probe→steer work operates at response level on short-form QA; RaS is the first to operate at claim level during long-form generation with calibrated (not binary) confidence expression.

**3. Address the orthogonality scaling gap explicitly:**
Don't claim orthogonality transfers — frame it as a hypothesis to test. Add a dedicated experiment: replicate Miao & Ungar's orthogonality analysis on your primary model (measuring cosine similarity between accuracy and confidence directions at 27B+ scale on long-form generation). This is both a contribution (extending the finding to new settings) and a risk-mitigation step.

**4. Target AAAI 2027 (July 28) instead of EMNLP (May 25):**
10 days is too tight for a paper with this many unvalidated assumptions. AAAI gives 10+ weeks, which allows: 1-week pilot on architecture/orthogonality, 3-week implementation, 2-week evaluation, 4-week writing. Still ambitious but feasible.

**5. Strengthen the impact argument:**
The crowded landscape (CURE, CAG, CSS, PCNET, LoVeC, Rewarding Doubt) means you need clear quantitative expectations. State upfront: 'We expect RaS to achieve claim-level ECE below X (vs. Y for unsteered and Z for binary clamping) while maintaining FActScore above W.' Without specific targets, the paper risks being 'we tried the obvious combination and it kind of worked.'

## Instructions
- Think in two phases: FIRST reconsider the problem framing (core_problem / opportunity / landscape) if the reviewer flagged issues there, THEN revise the method (approach / resource_estimate / key_references). Do not jump straight to fixing the method if the underlying problem framing needs correction.
- Address each issue specifically.

## 深度调研要求（每一轮修订都必须执行）

不要简单地'打补丁'——每一轮修订都是重新审视和深化这个 idea 的机会。

1. **深度搜索**：针对 reviewer 指出的每个问题，建议用 2-3 种不同的搜索查询调研。
   - 搜索最新的相关论文（arXiv, conference proceedings）
   - 搜索 benchmark/leaderboard 确认当前 SOTA
   - 搜索可能遗漏的相关工作和 concurrent work

2. **深度阅读**：用 WebFetch 实际阅读找到的关键论文的 abstract 和方法部分，
   不要只依赖搜索摘要。形成你自己对领域现状的独立判断。

3. **深度思考**：在修订之前，先独立思考以下问题：
   - 这个 idea 的核心假设是否仍然成立？
   - reviewer 的批评是否揭示了更深层的问题？
   - 有没有更好的 framing 或 approach 来解决同一个核心问题？
   - 修订后的 idea 相比上一版有什么本质性的改进？

4. **避免表面修订**：如果你发现自己只是在换措辞或补充细节而没有实质改进，
   考虑是否需要 major revision 或 pivot。反复的 minor fix 不会拯救一个根基有问题的 idea。

## 针对 Review 意见的定向搜索

对 reviewer 指出的每个问题，执行以下搜索流程：

1. **如果 reviewer 说'已有类似工作'**：
   - 搜索 reviewer 提到的论文，用 WebFetch 实际阅读
   - 搜索该论文的 cited-by，找到后续跟进工作
   - 明确你的 idea 与这些工作的差异化点——如果差异化不够，必须 pivot

2. **如果 reviewer 说'SOTA 过时'**：
   - 用 Papers With Code 查看当前排行榜
   - 搜索过去 6 个月的最新方法
   - 更新你的 landscape 和 baseline

3. **如果 reviewer 说'可行性有问题'**：
   - 搜索类似规模实验的实际成本和时间线
   - 搜索 GitHub 上是否有可复用的实现
   - 搜索相关数据集/模型的可获取性

4. **如果 reviewer 说'novelty 不足'**：
   - 对核心方法尽量做 3-5 种不同关键词组合的搜索
   - 搜索相邻领域是否有类似思路
   - 如果确实 novelty 不足，考虑 major revision 或 pivot

- Use WebSearch to find updated information if the reviewer flagged outdated claims.
- You have full freedom in how much to change:
  - Minor fix: if only specific details are wrong, correct them and keep everything else.
  - Major revision: if the approach is fundamentally flawed but the core problem is valid, you may redesign the approach entirely.
  - Pivot: if the reviewer's feedback reveals that the core problem itself is invalid (e.g., the gap no longer exists), you may propose a RELATED but substantially different idea that builds on the same research area. This is preferred over forcing a doomed idea to pass review.
- The output replaces the original idea (same tracking ID). Whether you make a small tweak or a full pivot, output a COMPLETE JSON object with ALL fields filled.
- In the output JSON, include a "change_type" field with one of: "minor", "major", or "pivot" to indicate the scope of your changes.
- Output the revised idea as a COMPLETE JSON object (same schema as original, plus "change_type").

## Qwen3.5-27B Architecture Overview

The Qwen3.5-27B is a 27-billion parameter dense hybrid model, representing a different approach from larger MoE variants in the Qwen3.5 family.

## Hybrid Linear Attention Design

Qwen3.5 introduces a hybrid architecture featuring Gated DeltaNet (linear attention) in 75% of layers. The model has 27B parameters distributed across 64 layers, with the hidden layout following a distinctive repeating pattern: 16 blocks, each structured as 3 × (Gated DeltaNet → FFN) → 1 × (Gated Attention → FFN), meaning three out of every four sublayers use Gated DeltaNet with only every fourth sublayer using standard Gated Attention.

## Technical Advantages

Traditional self-attention computes relationships between every token pair, which scales quadratically (O(n²)) with sequence length — expensive for long contexts. Linear attention mechanisms like DeltaNet approximate this with linear complexity (O(n)), making them significantly faster and more memory-efficient.

The Gated DeltaNet layers use a delta-rule update mechanism with a learned gating function, allowing the model to selectively update its recurrent state based on relevance. The standard Gated Attention layer that follows every three linear layers acts as a correction pass, catching anything the linear layers may have smoothed over.

## Performance and Context Window

Linear attention in the majority of layers keeps memory and compute manageable at 262K+ tokens, while standard attention at regular intervals preserves accuracy on tasks requiring exact token relationships.

## Overview

Inference-Time Intervention (ITI) is a technique designed to enhance the "truthfulness" of large language models by shifting model activations during inference, following a learned set of directions across a limited number of attention heads.

## Key Methodology

The approach works through linear probes and identifying truthful directions:

ITI identifies a sparse set of attention heads highly correlated with truthfulness by analyzing their linear probing accuracy on a labeled dataset. During text generation, ITI shifts activations within these identified attention heads along truth-correlated directions, repeating this process autoregressively for each token.

The method uses a mass mean shift to determine the optimal vector for activation manipulation, effectively guiding the model towards more truthful outputs.

## Performance Results

This intervention significantly improves the performance of LLaMA models on the TruthfulQA benchmark, and on an instruction-finetuned LLaMA called Alpaca, ITI improves its truthfulness from 32.5% to 65.1%.

## Advantages

ITI is minimally invasive and computationally inexpensive, and the technique is data efficient: while approaches like RLHF require extensive annotations, ITI locates truthful directions using only few hundred examples.

## Implications

The findings suggest that LLMs may have an internal representation of the likelihood of something being true, even as they produce falsehoods on the surface.

## Overview

The paper "Enhancing Language Model Factuality via Activation-Based Confidence Calibration and Guided Decoding" was presented at the 2024 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing.

## ActCab (Activation-based Confidence Calibration)

ActCab is an activation-based calibration method which trains a linear layer on top of the LM's last-layer activations that can better capture the representations of knowledge. By evaluating on five popular QA benchmarks, ActCab achieves superior calibration performance than all competitive baselines, e.g., by reducing the average expected calibration error (ECE) score by up to 39%.

## CoDec (Confidence-guided Decoding)

Built on top of ActCab, CoDec is a confidence-guided decoding strategy to elicit truthful answers with high confidence from LMs. More specifically, CoDec directs the LM to generate outputs with higher confidence by incorporating the confidence scores of candidate tokens with the top-K highest probabilities predicted by the LM, which increases the likelihood that the answers are correct while maintaining inference efficiency.

## Results on Factuality

Further experiments on CoDec show consistent improvements in several LMs' factuality on challenging QA datasets, such as TruthfulQA, highlighting the value of confidence signals in enhancing the factuality.

CAA is most effective when applied at early-mid layers, and the effectiveness of CAA diminishes with model size.

CAA is a method for steering language models by modifying their activations during forward passes. It computes "steering vectors" by averaging the difference in residual stream activations between pairs of positive and negative examples of a particular behavior, and these vectors are added at all token positions during inference with either a positive or negative coefficient.

## Context-Dependent Steering Mechanism

CLAS modulates steering strength through learned sensing vectors. The core formula is:

**h̃ℓ,t = hℓ,t + (cℓ · [hℓ,t 1]) dℓ**

Where the steering coefficient αℓ,t = (cℓ · [hℓ,t 1]) becomes block and context-dependent, rather than a fixed scalar. The sensing vectors {cℓ} are trained by minimizing next-token prediction loss on prompt-completion pairs, enabling the model to adapt steering strength based on input activations.

## Probe-Based Steering Vectors

Yes, CLAS uses probes for the steering direction extraction phase. It employs Recursive Feature Machines (RFMs) trained on labeled prompt-concept pairs to extract per-block steering vectors {dℓ}. # Transformer Interpretability Transfer to RNNs: Key Findings

## Overview
This research examined whether three major transformer interpretability techniques work on modern RNN architectures (Mamba and RWKV). The answer is generally yes, though with important nuances.

## What Works

**Contrastive Activation Addition (Steering)**
The method transfers to RNNs but with somewhat reduced effectiveness. The researchers found that "steering changes at most by 0.15 the probability of a Survival Instinct behavior" in Mamba, compared to 0.2 in transformers at similar scales. Some behaviors like sycophancy showed minimal steering effects across both architecture types.

**Tuned Lens (Latent Predictions)**
This technique successfully transfers. The authors confirmed that "perplexity decreases monotonically with depth" in RNNs just as in transformers, validating the iterative inference perspective across architectures.

**Eliciting Latent Knowledge (Quirky Models)**
Probes trained on "honest" model contexts generalized to deceptive contexts in RNNs, achieving over 70% AUROC—matching transformer performance on this task.

## Novel RNN-Specific Findings

The researchers introduced **state steering**, leveraging RNNs' compressed internal states. However, combining activation and state steering proved "not additive," suggesting the state is already influenced by activation changes.

## Key Limitation
The study focused on representation-based methods, explicitly excluding mechanistic or circuit-based interpretability approaches that might behave differently across architectures.

Based on my review of this paper, **it does not analyze interpretability techniques** such as linear probes, activation steering, or contrastive activation addition on hybrid linear attention models.

The paper's focus is strictly on architectural performance comparison and efficiency trade-offs. The authors examine:

- Language modeling performance across different linear attention variants
- Recall capabilities using the RULER benchmark
- How linear-to-full attention ratios affect performance
- Which architectural components (selective gating, hierarchical recurrence, controlled forgetting) matter most

The research provides no discussion of probing mechanisms, steering methods, or interpretability differences between DeltaNet/Gated DeltaNet layers versus standard attention layers in hybrid configurations.

## Key Gap

This represents an unexplored research direction. Given that hybrid models combine fundamentally different attention mechanisms—recurrent state-based layers versus full quadratic attention—investigating how interpretability techniques generalize (or fail to generalize) across these heterogeneous component types would be valuable future work.

, shows high steering resistance rates, and requires careful memory management—likely needing 2× H100s for inference
  
- **Qwen2.5-72B**: Standard transformer with 64 layers and GQA, known to work with SAE-based steering and probing, though smaller Qwen variants showed reduced sensitivity to confidence steering

- **Qwen2.5-32B**: Standard transformer with 64 layers and 32.5B parameters that fits comfortably on a single H100 80GB at FP16, offering a good balance between scale and practical constraints

- **Llama 3.1-8B**: Well-studied for VUF and steering with direct comparisons to prior work, providing a smaller validated baseline

The reviewer pushed for Llama 3.1-70B as the primary model, but I'm weighing the tradeoff: CAA effectiveness diminishes at larger scales, and the 70B variant shows significant endogenous steering resistance. Qwen2.5-32B might be the better primary choice—it's large enough to test scaling effects, uses standard transformer architecture, and fits on a single GPU without memory gymnastics.

Though actually, using 70B does make for a more compelling paper, and studying whether probe-guided steering works at that scale is itself a valuable contribution. So I'll go with Llama 3.1-70B as primary with Llama 3.1-8B for validation and Qwen2.5-32B as optional exploration across model families. That addresses the reviewer's feedback while building a coherent scaling narrative.

Now I need to think through what competitors I'm missing.

CORAL from Miao & Ungar's group uses MLP probes on residual activations to predict correctness and steer at inference, but it's limited to MCQA on 7B models—whereas my approach uses linear probes for longer-form generation at the claim level. CLAS adapts steering strength per-token based on context using learned sensing vectors, tested across multiple benchmarks and larger models like Llama 3.1-70B, but it doesn't focus on long-form calibration the way my method does.

ITI is the foundational work that identifies truthful directions in attention heads and shifts activations during generation, though it only targets TruthfulQA and aims to change content rather than calibrate confidence expression. ActCab and CoDec use linear layers on final activations for confidence calibration through decoding modifications, but they don't steer the verbalized confidence expression itself like my approach does.

The open question from Miao & Ungar is whether their linear encoding findings scale to larger models.

No one's actually tested this at 70B scale or in long-form generation contexts, so I should frame this as a hypothesis to validate—and that validation becomes a contribution. There's also LoVeC, an RL-based method for verbalized confidence in long-form text that's been tested on 8-9B models, which I should include as another training-based baseline.

For timing, EMNLP 2026 is essentially off the table with only 10 days left, but AAAI 2027 with its July deadlines is feasible at roughly 10 weeks out, making it the primary target alongside ICLR 2027.

On the scaling concern—CAA effectiveness does drop with model size according to recent scaling laws, and there's a 3.8% endogenous steering resistance at 70B that's worth taking seriously. But that scaling work used older Llama 2 architecture, whereas CLAS already demonstrated success on Llama-3.1-70B. The probe-guided approach might actually be more robust here since it can dynamically adjust steering intensity based on what the probe detects. For the resource side, running inference on Llama 3.1-70B in FP16 requires two H100 80GB GPUs, or I could use INT4 quantization on a single GPU, though that adds complexity to the probing pipeline.

The compute math is tighter than initially estimated—at roughly 20-30 tokens per second throughput, we're looking at around 250-300 H100-hours total. The real constraint is that probing needs full-precision access to hidden states, so tensor parallelism across two H100s becomes necessary. At spot pricing of $2.50-3.50 per H100 per hour, that's $5-7/hr for the pair. Looking back at what they actually want: a standard transformer baseline that's large enough to be meaningful, with the ability to compare directly to Miao & Ungar's work. The 8B model handles that comparison, and the 70B gives the scale they're after. I think the right move is to commit to both—8B for validation and direct comparison, 70B as the primary result—and accept that this pushes closer to 280 H100-hours.

Now I'm reconsidering the core assumptions underlying the whole approach. The central idea is that I can detect claim-level accuracy signals through probes while the model is generating, then adjust the verbalized confidence to match those signals. The first assumption to validate is whether factuality probes actually work during generation, not just on finished text. Han et al. demonstrated this works post-hoc on generated outputs, but I need to confirm it holds in the streaming case.

The second assumption—that accuracy and confidence are orthogonal at larger scales and in longer-form text—is the real vulnerability here. I've only seen this validated at 7-8B on QA tasks, and it's explicitly untested at bigger model sizes. That said, testing this orthogonality is itself a contribution. The third assumption is whether steering along the confidence direction produces natural-sounding hedging. Prior work shows ECE improvements and hallucination reduction, but the quality of long-form hedging and whether it sounds natural to humans remains unvalidated. Finally, I need to confirm that single-pass operation is actually feasible—the probe runs on hidden states already computed during generation, and steering happens at sentence boundaries rather than every token, which should be architecturally sound.

For the fifth assumption about steering not degrading content quality, orthogonality suggests it shouldn't, but scaling laws show CAA can have side effects at 70B. I'll need to measure factuality before and after steering to verify this. The core idea holds, but I should frame orthogonality verification as a contribution rather than a given, and acknowledge that CAA diminishing returns at scale is a legitimate concern.

Here is the complete revised idea as a JSON object. This is a **major revision** — the core probe→steer idea for claim-level long-form confidence calibration is preserved, but with critical changes to model selection, landscape coverage, experimental design, and framing.

---

## Summary of changes addressing each reviewer issue

**1. Qwen3.5-27B replaced (CRITICAL):** Switched to Llama 3.1-70B (primary) + Llama 3.1-8B (validation). Both are standard dense transformers with well-validated probing/steering support. Research confirms: (a) CLAS successfully tested probe-derived steering on Llama-3.1-70B across 11 benchmarks; (b) "Does Transformer Interpretability Transfer to RNNs?" shows probing/CAA have ~25% reduced effectiveness on recurrent architectures, motivating avoidance of Qwen 3.5's untested DeltaNet layers.

**2. All missing competitors cited and differentiated:**
- **ITI** (NeurIPS 2023): Foundational probe→steer — but targets truthfulness (content change) on TruthfulQA, not calibrated confidence expression in long-form
- **CORAL** (Feb 2026, same Miao & Ungar group): MLP probes→correctness steering on MCQA at 7B — response-level, not claim-level long-form
- **CLAS** (Apr 2026): Context-dependent adaptive steering via sensing vectors, tested on 70B — but general-purpose steering, not factuality-probe-driven confidence calibration
- **ActCab/CoDec** (EMNLP 2024): Activation calibration + guided decoding — modifies decoding probabilities, not verbalized confidence expression
- **LoVeC** (May 2025): RL-based long-form verbalized confidence — training-based (requires RL fine-tuning)

**3. Orthogonality framed as hypothesis with dedicated experiment:** Added an explicit ~8h pilot experiment replicating Miao & Ungar's analysis at 70B scale on long-form generation. Three outcomes defined: (a) holds → proceed + report scaling result; (b) partially holds → adapt with Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization; (c) fails → report as negative finding + fall back to 8B. All outcomes are publishable. The orthogonality verification itself is framed as a contribution.

**4. Timeline updated to AAAI 2027 primary:** Dropped EMNLP May 25 (impossible — 10 days away). Primary target: AAAI 2027 (Jul 28, ~10 weeks). Alternative: ARR August 3 (11 weeks, committable to EMNLP 2026). Backup: ICLR 2027 (~Oct 2026).

**5. Quantitative targets added:**
- Claim-level ECE reduction ≥40% over unsteered baselines
- FActScore preservation within 2% of unsteered baseline
- Uncertainty detection AUROC ≥0.80
- Superior calibration vs Han et al.'s binary clamping at comparable FActScore
- Targets explicitly discounted from Miao & Ungar's 70-90% response-level ECE reductions for the harder claim-level long-form setting

**6. Qwen sensitivity issue resolved:** By dropping Qwen entirely in favor of Llama-only experiments, the known issue of Qwen models' reduced sensitivity to confidence steering is no longer a concern.

**7. CAA scaling concerns addressed explicitly:** Acknowledged the ICML 2025 scaling laws finding (CAA diminishes at 70B) and the endogenous steering resistance phenomenon (3.8% ESR at 70B). Argued that (a) CLAS shows probe-derived adaptive steering works at 70B, (b) our probe-guided approach steers only when needed at calibrated intensity (not uniform CAA), and (c) the pilot experiment de-risks this before full budget commitment.

**8. Resource estimates updated:** ~250 H100-hours total for manual execution (~$625-875), reflecting the 2× H100 tensor parallelism requirement for 70B inference. Includes fallback plan reducing to ~80 H100-hours if the orthogonality pilot fails.

**Offline Stage 1 — Factuality Probe Training (~12h wall, 2× H100 for 70B; ~4h, 1× H100 for 8B; one-time per model):** Generate long-form outputs (biographies, factual descriptions) from the target model, decompose into atomic claims using FActScore/OpenFActScore decomposition, verify claim factuality against knowledge sources. Unlike Han et al.'s binary factuality labels, we train on soft labels derived from verification confidence, enabling graded uncertainty estimation.

**Offline Stage 2 — Verbalized-Confidence Direction Extraction (~5h wall, 2× H100 for 70B; ~2h, 1× H100 for 8B; one-time per model):** Extract a verbalized-confidence steering direction via contrastive activation pairs: generate matched claim pairs where the same factual content is expressed with high confidence ('X was born in Y') vs. hedged uncertainty ('X was reportedly born in Y, though I am not certain'). For the 70B model, if the pilot reveals partial orthogonality degradation, we apply Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization to project the confidence direction away from the accuracy direction before use.

(2) Maintain a running mean probe score over the current sentence span using a sliding window. (3) At sentence boundaries (detected from generated punctuation — periods, newlines — which are trivially available during generation), evaluate the accumulated probe score against a calibrated threshold. (4) If the probe indicates internal uncertainty (score below threshold) while the generation shows no hedging markers, apply a steering offset along the extracted verbalized-confidence direction on subsequent tokens, with steering magnitude α proportional to the miscalibration gap: α = β × max(0, threshold − probe_score), where β is calibrated on a held-out validation set. This adaptive formula is conceptually related to CLAS's context-dependent steering, but driven by per-claim factuality probe scores rather than general input-context sensing vectors. (5) Deactivate steering when the probe score recovers above threshold.

**Key design choices addressing known limitations:** (a) Span-aggregated probe scores over the full claim token range avoid the single-token prefix-contamination problem — the signal reflects the entire claim, not just the cumulative prefix. (b) Single-pass online monitoring eliminates the two-pass chicken-and-egg problem identified for the original CL-MUC approach — no position-aligned regeneration needed. (c) Continuous calibrated steering (not binary neuron clamping) produces graded hedging proportional to internal uncertainty, distinguishing this from Han et al.'s binary intervention. (d) Operating on the verbalized-confidence direction (orthogonal to accuracy per Miao & Ungar, verified at 70B scale in our pilot) means steering affects expression style without corrupting the model's factual knowledge.
